name: Belgian Amber Ale
description: Antwerp's house beer: copper-coloured, lightly fruity and built for the second and third glass. Ordered by the glass shape rather than the name.
funFact: In Antwerp you order it by asking for a 'bolleke' — the round stemmed glass — rather than by the brewery's name, which is one of the few places a glass has become the name of the drink.

serve.how: Serve in a round stemmed glass, filled to leave a proper two fingers of foam, and drink it cool rather than cold. The malt is the point: toasted and biscuity with just enough hop to keep it moving. It is a session beer by Belgian standards, so pour it with the expectation of ordering another rather than contemplating one.

composition.summary: A copper Belgian ale balancing toasted malt against a restrained ale-yeast fruitiness.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale and Vienna malts with a touch of caramel for copper colour.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Continental hops at modest, balancing levels.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: A Belgian ale strain kept deliberately restrained — fruit, not spice.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Nothing — this is a plain beer by Belgian standards.

composition.process: Warm-fermented with a house Belgian strain and conditioned cool so the malt stays forward.

name: Bokbier
description: The Dutch autumn bock: dark, malty and released each October, when the whole country's breweries put one out at once.
funFact: Dutch bokbier is a seasonal event rather than a year-round style — the Bokbierfestival in Amsterdam exists to taste the year's releases side by side, and most disappear by December.

serve.how: Serve cool rather than cold, in a tulip that holds the malt aroma. Pour to a modest head and give it a few minutes; the raisin and toast notes need a little warmth to separate from the alcohol. It is an autumn beer by design and pairs with the heavier food of that season rather than anything light.

composition.summary: A dark, malt-forward seasonal lager brewed to a bock strength.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Munich and caramel malts over a pale base for depth and colour.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low, present only to keep the malt from cloying.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Seasonal release — traditionally brewed for autumn only.

composition.process: Cold-fermented on a heavy Munich-and-caramel grist, then lagered for weeks before an autumn release.

name: Bière Bretonne
description: Brittany's revived brewing tradition: often buckwheat-inflected, sometimes seaweed-salted, and always defined against the cider the region is better known for.
funFact: Breton brewing was effectively extinct by the 1970s and was rebuilt from scratch in the 1980s as part of the wider Breton cultural revival — the beers carry Breton-language names as a deliberate political statement.

serve.how: Serve cool in a wide glass so the buckwheat and toasted character can open. Expect an amber to dark pour with a soft, bready body rather than a crisp one. It suits the region's food directly — buckwheat galettes and shellfish — and drinks better alongside a meal than on its own.

composition.summary: A revived regional French ale often built on buckwheat alongside barley malt.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt with a proportion of buckwheat, the regional grain.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Continental, moderate and herbal rather than citric.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Ale yeast fermented warm for a soft, bready profile.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Occasionally seaweed or salt, reflecting the coastal setting.

composition.process: Warm ale fermentation on a mixed barley-and-buckwheat grist, conditioned briefly and sold regionally.
